chapter_theme: The woman puts her own eyes on trial. They showed her the man, so they caused the sickness; now they weep, can't sleep and betray her secret, and she answers with bitter laughter and a curse. Blaming a body part makes her suffering speakable.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's, almost all spoken to her friend. The eyes are addressed in the third person throughout, and the argument moves from accusation (1171-1173) to satisfaction at their punishment (1174-1177) to their sleeplessness and their betrayal of her (1178-1180).

1171.reading: The woman asks why her eyes weep, when it was they who showed him to her, and so she came to know this unending sickness.
1171.nuance: The verse says 'we saw the sickness' with no mention of him, and the object of 'showed' has to be supplied, as Parimelazhagar says. In her account, seeing him and seeing the sickness are the same act.

1172.reading: The woman asks why these kohl-lined eyes, which looked as they did, now suffer in misery without coming to terms with it.

positions.position: தெரிந்துணரா means they looked without considering what would follow, so they should now bear what they caused.
positions.quote: மேல் விளைவதனை ஆராய்ந்தறியாது அன்று காதலரை நோக்கி நின்ற உண்கண்கள்

positions.position: It means the opposite: they looked after judging him good, and now they no longer recognise that goodness.
positions.quote: முன்பு அவர் நல்லரென்று தெரிந்து உணர்ந்து நோக்கிய உண்கண் கள்

1173.reading: The woman says it's laughable that her eyes looked at him so quickly on their own and now weep on their own.
1173.nuance: The repeated தாம் is the whole charge: they acted of their own accord both times. Manakkudavar pictures real laughter, a distracted woman laughing through her distress and being asked why, which makes this more disturbing than wit.

1174.reading: The woman says her kohl-lined eyes, having fixed in her an inescapable, fatal sickness, have dried up and can no longer even weep.
1174.nuance: Dry eyes come after much weeping. What seems a relief is presented as the eyes' punishment: in Parimelazhagar's words, harm they did her has come back to them by itself.

1175.reading: The woman says her eyes, which gave her a sickness too large for the sea, now suffer torments and can't sleep.
1175.nuance: The commentators use the language of moral consequence with some wit: Parimelazhagar says அத் தீவினையால், 'by that evil deed', and Manakkudavar has harm returning to those who harm others. The verse just shows the sequence.

1176.reading: The woman exclaims how sweet it is that the eyes that gave her this sickness have fallen into it themselves.
1176.nuance: Vengeance against one's own organ can only hurt the avenger, and that absurdity is the point. Parimelazhagar's gloss, 'as if my suffering had ended', keeps the distance between the delight and any real relief.

1177.reading: The woman curses them: may the eyes that longed and melted and begged to see him suffer on until their inner water is gone.
1177.nuance: The verse echoes itself: உழந்துழந்து against விழைந்திழைந்து, suffering matching longing in the same rhythm. Pay-back is built into the sound.

1178.reading: The woman says there is one who desired without cherishing, and her eyes can't be at peace without seeing him.
1178.nuance: The syntax allows several readings, and the second one Parimelazhagar gives rests on a different text, கொண்கனை. I'm unsure which is best. The steady part is the last clause: whatever he is, the eyes can't do without him.

positions.position: The friend says he hasn't really gone away. She replies: yes, someone who loved in words and not at heart is here, but what use is that if the eyes don't see him?
positions.quote: நெஞ்சால் விழையாது வைத்துச் சொல் மாத்திரத்தால் விழைந்தவர் இவ்விடத்தே உளர்

positions.position: It's a question, with no claim that he's near: does anyone desire what shouldn't be desired? He has gone without wishing to see them, and the eyes still can't settle.

1179.reading: The woman says that when he doesn't come her eyes don't sleep, and when he does they still don't sleep, so either way they suffer terribly.
1179.nuance: Parimelazhagar supplies the two reasons: they stay up watching for him, and when he is there they stay up for fear he'll leave. Kalaignar's gloss reads this more generally, as the lot of all lovers' eyes.

1180.reading: The woman says it isn't hard for the town to learn the secret in the hearts of those like her, whose eyes are beaten drums.
1180.nuance: The eyes' final offence is treason. The friend has asked her to hide his cruelty so the town won't blame him, and she answers that the eyes make that impossible. Parimelazhagar notes the variant reading அறைபறைக் கண்ணார், which removes the poetic strain.

links.note: 1076 calls base men a beaten drum because they carry secrets to others. 1180 uses the same அறைபறை for her own eyes. An image of contempt for informers becomes an image of her helplessness: her body is what informs on her.

319 says harm done to others in the morning comes back to you by itself in the afternoon. Manakkudavar's gloss on 1175 uses this same moral logic, with the eyes as offenders. A serious doctrine is applied, playfully, to a woman's own eyes.

1170 wishes the eyes could travel to him as the heart does. Next, 1171 begins the attack on them. Parimelazhagar explicitly calls 1170 a preparation for this chapter, so what looks like a change of subject is a single thought.

source_issues: 1178: Parimelazhagar reports a variant, கொண்கனை, with a different reading attached.
